lines.note: Songǒ is an honored name, explained by tattoqi na and a sacred, exalted name. The scan supplies the second t in Tattoqi and the ct sequence in ſancto; the final S is a separate upright label.

Songuai is outside the village or settlement. The worn consonant in foca is read as c rather than the draft's t, consistent with the clearly outdoor Portuguese gloss; the village noun in Portuguese is pouoação.
Songuen refers to honored speech or words. The Japanese cotoba supports the Portuguese Palaura, whose sacred or honorific qualification continues below.
This completes the speech entry by specifying words of a high-ranking, noble person. The register label remains upright after the italic gloss.
Songuiǒ is an honored form or image. The Portuguese begins figure or statue and divides estatua at the physical line end; the headword has a caron, not a circumflex.

runs.text: tua de peßoa nobre, ou ſancta como Fotoque.

lines.note: The statue represents a noble or sacred person, such as a Buddhist sacred figure. Fotoque is embedded in this Portuguese explanation and is not a new Japanese example.
Son-i concerns an honored person's heart or intention. The printed hyphen distinguishes this occurrence from the separately spaced Son i entry below; the phrase continues on the next two rows.

runs.text: ſancto, & nobre. Item, Mandado, ou vontade

lines.note: This completes the sacred and noble man's heart and adds command or will. The scan has nobre and vontade rather than the draft's mobre and contade; the ct ligature in sancto is not a long-s sequence.
The command or will belongs to a high-ranking person. The stop before &c. is retained rather than silently changing the source punctuation to a comma.
This second son-i is an honored rank or dignity, paraphrased by tattoqi curai. The source spacing in Son i is retained, and the Portuguese pessoa is split between two long-s types on adjacent rows.
The continuation finishes pessoa alta, a person of high rank. It belongs to the dignity entry and is not merged with the wine-vessel entry below.

runs.text: Diante, ou junto da barça de vinho.

lines.note: This Sonjen is being before or beside the vessel of wine. The Portuguese vinho and the e in the headword are legible corrections to the draft's vinbo and Sonjan; barça is preserved rather than replaced by a modern vessel name.
A second Sonjen means in the presence of a high or sacred person. Its repeated spelling is intentional; the definition continues with an example on the next row.
The example describes putting or presenting something before the honored person. The nasal abbreviation in apreſẽ- is preserved at the division into apresentar.

runs.text: tar diante da peßoa alta, & ſancta.

lines.note: This completes the Portuguese presentation formula. The sacred qualification belongs to the person before whom something is placed, and S remains a separate register label.
Sonji here denotes little grandchildren, explicitly identified by mago. This is a noun distinct from the similarly spelled verb on the following row; the apparatus after i is a comma.
The verb sonji means becoming damaged or failing. The Portuguese begins a grammatical explanation of attaching this verb to others; the printed division ver-bo is retained.

runs.text: bo com a raiz de muitos, & ſignifica errar

lines.note: The grammatical note says the verb attaches to the root of many other verbs and adds the meaning of doing something wrongly. This is running Portuguese, not a new entry.

runs.text: no fazer a couſa que ſignifica a raiz. Vt,

lines.note: The relevant error concerns performing the action denoted by the root. Italic Vt introduces the examples that follow on separate physical rows.
Caqi sonzuru illustrates making a mistake in writing. Yo- begins the reading example on the following row; its hyphen is visible and is not removed to join the word.

The opening miſonzuru completes yomi-sonzuru, making a reading error. The next example has a fish as its subject; Iuoga is the historical spelling retained here, not silently changed to a modern form.
Jita completes sonjita: the fish has spoiled or gone bad. The Portuguese gives both becoming damaged and corrupted; the historical corrompeoſe spelling is preserved.
Sonin and Sojin are alternatives for an ordinary person, explained as tadano fito. The Portuguese comum is split after co-, while the alternative marker l remains separate from the headword.
This finishes comum and adds ordinary as a second equivalent. The line is a short continuation of the common-person entry, with its own crop and indentation.
This Sonin is a complainant or accuser, described as the person bringing a suit. Vttayuru retains its historical spelling, while autor has the legal sense of plaintiff in the continuation.
The short phrase completes autor na demanda, the plaintiff in a lawsuit. It belongs to the legal Sonin entry rather than the following diviner entry.

Sǒnin is a diviner, explicitly a person practicing divination. The scan resolves the draft's badly corrupted Japanese as Vranai ſuru fito. Second-pass enlargement distinguishes two dotted i-types, one before and one after u, establishing the Portuguese Adiuinho; the historical u is not modernized to v.
This completes feiticeiro, the second Portuguese equivalent for the diviner. The word is physically divided after fei- on the preceding row.
Sonjin means a person of the village or settlement. Muranofito remains joined as in the source, and the Portuguese uses an unexpanded tilde in Homẽ.
Sonmei is an honored command or instruction. The circumflex in vôxe is retained, and the Portuguese pessoa is divided after its first long s.
This completes the command given by a high-ranking person. The separate physical continuation is preserved rather than joined to Sonmei's first row.
Sonmǒ directs the reader to Sonbǒ and gives loss or damage. Vide, not Vile, is the italic cross-reference instruction; the referenced Japanese headword is upright.

Sǒnǒ and Sǒnacu are alternative expressions for acting without giving a reason or with no further difficulty. Both carons are visible in the first form; the Portuguese explanation continues on later rows.

runs.text: mais nada, ou ſem muito negocio, ou traba-

lines.note: The gloss adds without anything further, much business, or trouble. Trabalho is divided at the printed hyphen and is not a separate entry.
The example says something was taken without giving a reason. The tilde in ſẽ is retained without expanding sem, and the Japanese past passive torareta remains upright.
The first phrase finishes the unexplained-taking example. The second says a boat arrived readily or without difficulty; tçuita is retained with its cedilla rather than modernized.

runs.text: Chegou a ẽbarcação facilmente, & ſẽ trabalho.

lines.note: The boat arrived easily and without trouble. The scan shows ẽbarcação with a tilde abbreviation, not the draft's cbarcação; both nasal marks are preserved.
Sono is a garden or cultivated plot. The Portuguese Iardim retains consonantal I, while the following horta is a second equivalent, not Japanese material.
Sonobun is adverbial, meaning in that manner. The source's Adu. label and joined double-s form in Deßa are preserved.
Sonocami refers to former times or formerly. The Portuguese explicitly gives an adverbial past-time meaning, distinguishing it from other sono- expressions.

Sonocoto is glossed both as that is so and that thing. The final vowel of the first Portuguese word is i, not the draft's a. Enlargement shows the close-set double-s shape; the aligned ß representation is retained, with separately set ſs a possible graphic alternative, rather than normalized to modern assim.
Sonofǒ can address another person or indicate that side. The final caron and the capital E in the second Portuguese meaning are retained.
Sonogotocu means in that manner. The headword's o vowels and the Portuguese adverb label are clearly supported by the scan.
Sonomama is likewise an adverb referring back to the preceding in-that-manner gloss. The worn second letter is o rather than the draft's u; Idem does not begin a new Japanese entry.
Sonomi means the person himself. A visible word division separates Elle and meſmo; this unaccented headword contrasts with Sônomi on the next row.
Sônomi is the whole body, a different expression from the preceding himself. The circumflex is part of the printed distinction and is not flattened to an unmarked o.
Sono miguiri means at that time or juncture. The source has initial S, a final i after r, and Portuguese Neße; these replace the draft's corrupted Bono miguir and Neſie.

Sonotçure concerns that sort or kind, not a geographical league. The Portuguese reads Deßa laya, and the example begins sonotçure no before continuing with mono below; the printed stop after Vt is retained.
Mono completes the example meaning a thing of that sort. The joined s form in deßa is read from the complete glyph rather than dropping its short-s component as in the draft.
Sonotoqi means at that time, glossed as then. The Portuguese adverb label and nasal mark in Então are retained.
Sonotǒza specifies the time immediately in question, rendered as then at present. The length mark is a caron and the Portuguese long s in preſente is preserved.
Sonoyǒni means in that way or manner. It is another adverbial sono- expression, not an inflected form of the preceding time word.
Sonpi contrasts the honored and lowly, matching tattoi and iyaxij. The Portuguese uses the conjunction e here rather than an ampersand; the terminal ij in the Japanese gloss is retained.
Sonpô is an honorific reply to a letter, explained by fumi no fenji. The scan's tall s in the st sequence is restored in Repoſta; the headword has a circumflex.

runs.text: pera peßoa nobre, ou que vem de peßoa nobre.

lines.note: The reply is addressed to, or comes from, a noble person. Pera is the source's historical preposition and is not normalized to para.
The example politely acknowledges seeing the correspondent's reply. Sonpô, not Sonnô, repeats the headword; the mǒxi and ſǒrǒ marks are carons, whereas Sonpô retains its circumflex.

runs.text: bi a repoſta de voßa mercè: quando hum res

lines.note: This completes recebi, acknowledging the addressee's reply, then begins an explanation of letter-writing practice. Second-pass enlargement establishes a single diagonal grave accent in mercè, not the draft's tilde; the following colon is visible. No unestablished hyphen is added after res.

runs.text: ponde por carta a peßoa alta eſcreue ſe eſta pa-

lines.note: The sentence concerns replying by letter to a high-ranking person and writing this word on the superscription. The separate eſcreue ſe and printed pa- division remain in physical order.
This completes palaura and places the expression in the letter's superscription. Sobre eſcrito remains two source words, not a modernized compound.
Sonqi is an honorific or sacred qualification. The Portuguese calls it a word used to honor someone; the ct sequence in Sancto is preserved.
The explanation says the word honors and elevates someone. The final S is an upright register label, not part of the Portuguese clause.
Sonqiǒ means veneration, corresponding to honoring and revering in the Japanese paraphrase. The final m in vyamǒ is partly worn but retained; l introduces an alternative Portuguese equivalent below.

The alternative is reverence, followed by a respectful Japanese expression for honoring God. The raised nine-shaped abbreviation after De is preserved as ꝰ, as on the preceding page; it is not a caron over o as the draft's Dǒuo implied.
Ru completes the respectful verb and the gloss says to honor or venerate God. The fully spelled Portuguese Deos is distinct from the abbreviated form inside the preceding Japanese example.
Sonqio is an honored pardon or permission, as yuruxi confirms. Portuguese Perdam is the historical pardon term here, not a loss; the first s of pessoa is followed by a printed hyphen.
The continuation specifies pardon from a noble person. It completes the split peſ-ſoa without relocating either part of the word.
Sonriǒ is an honored soul or spirit, corresponding to tamaxij. The gloss divides eſpiritu after eſ-, and the caron on the headword remains distinct from the nearby circumflexes.

runs.text: piritu de peßoa nobrej a morta.

lines.note: The spirit belongs to a noble person already dead. The source's tight nobrej and separation before a are preserved from the aligned draft, although the sense is nobre ja morta; the spacing is not silently modernized.
This Sonrǒ is the village elder, paraphrased as mura no toshiyori. The Portuguese begins old man or principal head and divides cabeça at the row end.
The row completes cabeça and identifies the principal elder of a settlement. The tilde remains over u in dalgũa, without editorial expansion.

The second Sonrǒ instead means an honored elder. The initial character in toxiyori is the worn t with its high crossbar, not the draft's long s; the different Japanese paraphrase separates the two homographs.
The honored elder may alternatively be described as sacred. This short row finishes the second Sonrǒ entry and is not part of the following work or action entry.
Sonſacu is an honored person's work or action, explained by xoſa. The long s in both Japanese forms is upright; the Portuguese explanation remains wholly italic.
Sonſat is an honorific word for a letter from a high-ranking person. Its final t is retained rather than expanded to a modern Japanese syllable.
Sonſô denotes revering or honoring, with tattomi and tattomu as Japanese equivalents. Camis begins in the Portuguese gloss and is physically divided after Ca-; the circumflex remains as printed.
This completes Camis and adds Buddhist sacred figures as objects of veneration. Fotoques is a whole Japanese-derived term embedded in Portuguese; the split Camis is not mistaken for a new entry.
Sontai is an honored body or sacred substance. The source has ſuſtancia without b, which is retained; corpo is divided after cor-.
This completes the body of a royal or noble person. The Portuguese real has the royal sense in this context, and the historical abbreviation &c. is preserved.
Sontǒ is an honored answer, corresponding to cotaye. The printed caron and the long s in Repoſta remain distinct features of the Japanese and Portuguese spans.
The answer is from a noble or sacred person. The visible separation between ou and ſancta is restored from the draft's accidental joining.
Sontocu pairs loss and benefit. The Portuguese proueito retains u for the consonantal value represented by modern v.
Sonuô denotes a noble elder, with voqina as the Japanese explanatory noun. The two t types in Tattoqi and the circumflex over the final o are preserved.
This Sonxi is an honored master or teacher. The Portuguese adds a usage qualification about respectful speech, continued below; xixǒ has a caron.
This completes the instruction that the title is used with reverence. The separate upright S label is retained after the italic usage note.

runs.text: Liuro que trata da arte militar.

lines.note: The second Sonxi names a book dealing with military art, distinct from the preceding teacher title. No author or expanded modern title is inserted into the transcription.
Sonxin is an honorific term for a person's heart or intention, explained by cocoro. The Portuguese sentence continues below and is not a separate gloss of the military book.
The single adjective completes the noble-person qualification of Sonxin. The final register label remains upright.

This entry denotes loss or damage and refers to Son. The first glyph has an S-shaped lower bowl, not the cedilla of the draft's ç; it is unusually low-set and lowercase-sized, so sonxit is retained with a nonblocking caveat about its case rather than silently promoted from a lexical index.
Sonxo is an honored letter, explained by tattoqi xo. The source separates those two Japanese words and has initial T, correcting the draft's Iattoqixo.

runs.text: Santo ſenhor: não ſe vſa ſe não falã-

lines.note: Sonxu is glossed as holy lord, with a restriction on its use. The source has Santo without c here, and the Portuguese uſa retains initial v as printed.

runs.text: do de Deos nos liuros da Igreja.

lines.note: The restriction is that the term is used of God in Church books. This completes the divided falando and retains Deos and Igreja as printed.
Sonxucu first denotes an honored residence or holy house. The tildes in Sãta and Itẽ are abbreviations, and the paragraph sign introduces an additional personal sense below.

runs.text: Peßoa nobre, ou de quem ſe fala com reuerẽcia.

lines.note: The additional meaning is a noble person or someone spoken of with reverence. The whole row is Portuguese, including its final nasal abbreviation in reuerẽcia.

Sonye refers to severe damage or destruction, corresponding to the two Japanese explanatory verbs. The Portuguese destruição continues below the last regular OCR row; that body continuation must not be retained as a catchword.

This is the missing body continuation of deſ-truição in the Sonye entry. It is restored to the second column under its existing ID; the separate right-hand Sonyeqi. is a catchword, not part of this gloss.
The right-hand catchword is Sonyeqi.; its worn n is read from the native bottom context. It is separated from truição, which completes the preceding body entry.
